title: Dividend and index investing

overview.objective: Own a broad slice of the market for years, with low costs and reinvested dividends.
overview.context: Long-term saving in shares through low-cost funds. Not a short-term trading method.

simple.simple: Instead of picking shares, buy an [[index-fund]] that holds many companies. Add a fixed amount on a schedule, reinvest the [[dividend|dividends]], keep fees low and hold for years.
simple.balanced: [[diversification|Diversification]] across many companies reduces the damage any one can do, but the fund still falls when the whole market falls, sometimes by a lot and for years. Fees are taken every year whatever the result, so small differences compound. [[dividend-yield|Dividend yield]] is income, not a forecast of price.

reasoning: Over long periods, the combined profits of many companies may grow, and owning a share of all of them avoids having to pick winners. That is the reasoning, not a promise; markets can fall and stay down for many years.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not anyone's documented method
rules: Invest a fixed amount on a fixed schedule into a broad, low-cost index fund.
Compare yearly fees before buying, and prefer the lower fee for the same index.
Rebalance once a year if you hold more than one fund.
Use only money you will not need for many years.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional plan? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional fund. You invest 200 a month for 3 months, at prices of 50, 40 and 50 per unit. Ignore fees.

options.text: Your average cost is about 46.15, below the simple average price of 46.67
options.explanation: Right: 600 ÷ 13 ≈ 46.15, and (50 + 40 + 50) ÷ 3 ≈ 46.67. A fixed amount buys more units when the price is low.

options.text: Investing all 600 at the first price of 50 would have bought more units
options.explanation: No: 600 ÷ 50 = 12 units, one fewer than the 13 bought month by month.

options.text: At a price of 50, the holding is worth 650
The dividend yield tells you the price will rise
options.explanation: No: yield is income relative to price, not a forecast.

failureAnalysis: A broad market fall takes the whole fund down, sometimes for years.
Needing the money during a fall forces selling at a loss.
High fees quietly reduce results every year.
limitations: Taxes and fees vary and are not included in the examples.
No claim is made about future market returns.
This page describes a principle, not advice for your situation.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share costs 40 and pays a yearly dividend of 1.60. What is the dividend yield?

options.explanation: No: that is 40 ÷ 1.60. Yield is the dividend divided by the price.

options.text: 1.6%, since the yield is just the dividend amount written as a percent
options.explanation: No: the dividend has to be divided by the price.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does a broad index fund not protect you from?

options.explanation: No: one company is a small part of a broad fund.

options.text: A fall in the whole market
options.explanation: Right: if the market falls, the fund falls with it.

options.text: One sector falling while the rest of the market rises
options.explanation: No: a broad fund holds many sectors, so one sector falling does limited damage.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Two funds track the same index. One charges 1.0% a year, the other 0.2%. Over many years…

options.text: They end level, because they hold the same shares
options.explanation: No: the fee gap is taken every year.

options.text: The 1% fund ends ahead, because a higher fee buys better tracking
options.explanation: No: a higher fee is not a sign of better results for the same index.

options.text: The 0.8 point gap is lost each year and compounds, so the cheaper fund is likely to end ahead
options.explanation: Right: same index, so the fee difference is most of the gap.
